text: Hi, everyone.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I'm Varun.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I'm one of the co-founders at LongLake.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And I'm excited to share a little bit about what we've been up to for the last two years.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It all comes back to a question all of us have asked time and time again.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The models are getting better, but the real question is, how do you actually deploy the AI into the real world?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: How do you get the models to complete economically relevant tasks?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Let me start by saying everyone has seen the demo.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Think of the agent automatically booking a flight, the agent automatically completing a ticket in some kind of customer service portal.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Think of an agent completing a block of code ready to commit and go.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The reality is we've all seen this, and it feels like magic.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Two years ago, any of this would have been complete science fiction.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The capabilities are real.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Now, walk with me into a 200-person property management firm.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Real people, real properties, real dollars, real customers all across the US.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You would expect AI to show up by now, but the reality is nothing has changed at all.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Here's the thing.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This is totally normal.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And maybe, in fact, I'd argue this is what we should expect.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This is true for every general purpose technology.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Take electricity, for example.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Electricity was invented in the 1880s, and it was first demoed at Edison's Pearl Street Station Dynamo Room over in Manhattan.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This was the magic demo of its time.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The reality is it took a long time for electricity to be fully adopted.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Consider a Ford factory.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's not enough to just have electricity.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You have to rip out the existing motors and equipment.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You have to bring in the new equipment.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You have to go and train everybody to use that very same equipment.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Here's a picture of a Ford electrified moving assembly in 1924.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: These things take time.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Diffusion of any technology takes a generation.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And since everyone here in this room today is talking about AI, I would argue AI diffusion is perhaps the single most important problem for the next 20 years.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The models are going to keep getting better.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The big question is, how do we actually get these models to be in the real world, complete real tasks, and make people more efficient, happier, and provide better service?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So taking a quick step back, who are we?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We are LongLake.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Over the last two years, we've raised over $3 billion from Elad Gill, General Catalyst, and AlphaWave since our founding.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Here's the strange part.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We don't sell software.

text: We actually go out and acquire and partner with real services businesses in the world.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We've acquired 35 businesses across HOA and property management, architecture, HR services, and a lot more.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: To give you a little bit more flavor, we have roughly a 40-person team right now, split between technology, finance, and operations.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: More than half our team is part of the technology team, focused on building products, data, and deploying the core products into the field.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We're in a collective group of folks, a bunch of ex-founders who've worked in the services before, ex-military folks from Palantir, Ramp, Glean, and from the finance side, Blackstone, HIG, et cetera.

text: We are not selling them to these companies above from the outside.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We're actually deploying into these companies and figuring out how to get the technology to work.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And just to show you the scale we're playing at, we announced recently our $6.3 billion take private of American Express Global Business Travel, the world's largest corporate travel platform.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We own these businesses.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So when the AI doesn't work, it's not their problem.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We're not the vendor.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's our problem.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Concretely, again, we are not the vendor.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We are the operator owners.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And we work very closely with our teams within the businesses to drive real outcomes.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Now I want to step back and get to the concrete about the how.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: What are the lessons we've learned over the last two and a half years and what we've learned from deploying AI into companies we've owned?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Three quick lessons.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: One, how we move agents from co-pilots to co-workers.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Two, how we leverage real-world data within these businesses.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Remember, we're seeing all of the work that's being done in these real services businesses.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: There's a lot of interesting problems and solutions embedded within that.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then finally, perhaps the most interesting and exciting is how do you actually get all of this technology to compound over time by learning loops in the enterprise?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And we'll get to that at the end over here.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So starting off from Copilots to coworkers.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: There's a spectrum of how much autonomy you can give an agent.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: On the left here, you see a Copilot.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This is your simple RAG chatbot from two years ago.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's very quick.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You can ask a question.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Maybe it's integrated with some systems.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It can give you information back very, very quickly.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The second step is a synchronous agent.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Consider something like Claude Code, Codex, ClaudeCowork.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's real-time.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: There's this two-way interaction.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's a bit more sophisticated than a Copilot.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You can go let it run off for one to five minutes.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It'll call tools, maybe use its skills.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's still synchronous.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You still need to step in and ask a query.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So the next obvious rung of the ladder is the asynchronous agent.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You can come in here, still ask a query.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The agent will go off into the background, do some work, and then come back.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And what's really interesting about asynchronous agents is that the user does not have to be the one that triggers them.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You can have external triggers as well.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Maybe someone completes a certain task and there is an async job queue that allows the async agent to pull off from and proactively offer advice to the end user.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Then I'd argue the next step is a long-running agent.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: How do you get these agents to work for hours, days, weeks, months, et cetera?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I think this is currently a very core problem that a lot of the labs are focused on, as are we.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then finally, at the end, the holy grail, an AI coworker.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This is where most people start off.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You want a proactive partner that gets work done just alongside you.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This is what everyone wants to sell you.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But what we've learned from owning the outcomes in this business is you have to earn the right to do more.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's not enough to jump to the coworker immediately for a bunch of reasons.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: One, for certain tasks, the models might not quite be there yet.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And two, you actually have to work with these companies in the field, interact and iterate very, very closely so that they understand that this is the beginning of AI and you can work up the rungs over time.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I think a really unique lens to look at this problem through is that of the jagged frontier.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We all know that agents are incredibly good at writing code.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So what does the, for example, synchronous agent for code generation look like?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This is super simple.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This is just your coding agent, maybe it's Codex, Claude Code, just running on your desktop.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It has access to a file system, you collaborate with it in real time, you get instant feedback, and you iterate.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The next step is if you look at code generation, what is the async agent?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This is also fairly straightforward and largely solved.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You take the exact same coding agent, you wrap it in a sandbox, and you just let it go run.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It can build, it can test, and once it's done with its work, it can provide the code in the form of a PR.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: One thing that's really unique about engineers is folks are incredibly good at already parallelizing their work.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's very commonplace to launch 10 jobs and be comfortable with the fact that job seven might finish before job three.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So engineers are incredibly good at using these async agents.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Now when we come to services, the equivalent of a synchronous agent, what we talked about a little bit earlier, it's a co-working agent.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's an agent that has deep context about your enterprise.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It interacts potentially with MCPs, custom tools, custom integrations, and you can chat with it synchronously just like any of these other products.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I think this is the frontier here in the bottom right.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: What does it mean to build an asynchronous agent for the services?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: What does it mean to parallelize work in industries where work is traditionally done in a very, very serial manner?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This is where we spend a lot of time, and this is what I wake up every morning really excited thinking about.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We've figured out what the async and forking mechanism for code is.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You just spin up a bunch of sandboxes and do work.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: What does that look like for the rest of the world?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So here's a couple questions we think about pretty seriously.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: One, the models are trained on code.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: They want to write code.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: They're incredibly good at writing code.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: How do we leverage these coding agents for actual knowledge work?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Rather than wait for the models to catch up on doing services knowledge work, what if we just use that code knowledge and represent knowledge work as code?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Two, as I mentioned, engineers are used to parallelizing work.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: How do you parallelize work that's traditionally serial?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: People clean out their inbox one email by one email, not 10 emails at once.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And finally, how do you move up the ladder here, both in terms of product and user enablement?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: What are the right form factors?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And I'd argue this varies dramatically from industry to industry.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Just because you have one way of launching an async agent for code doesn't mean that same way is going to work for architecture or property management.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The second point I want to cover today is leveraging real-world data.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We all know this.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Frontier models have learned from everything humanity has written down, but the most valuable tasks are not on the internet.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: How do you actually close the books when you're missing receipts?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: How do you scope a building for construction in a blueprint, potentially collaboratively?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: How do you coordinate vendors for fixing a broken roof?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: All of this knowledge lives in people's heads, in 20-year-old software, in the way that one senior person on one of these teams just knows how to do it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: How do you make this information explicit and create tasks that you can actually learn from?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So we've constructed a little bit of a flywheel.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We get our agents to collaborate with our employees to do real work.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And this allows us to generate rich traces of data and information, tool calls, the hiccups, the paper cuts, everything that goes wrong with doing real work.

speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Did the books get closed?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And what's really exciting is it ratchets up.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So our agents get better and better over time.

speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: One, we get to generate amazing evals that are built and scored automatically, and we're able to gather both implicit and explicit feedback.

text: Now on to the final thing I want to chat with you guys today is learning loops within the enterprise.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I'd argue there's two hot trends everyone's talking about in 2026.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: One, it's continual learning.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: How do you make an agent better over time with feedback?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I think there are plenty of sessions this week on how you can use continual learning, whether it's in the prompt or in the waits.

text: And two, enablement.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: How do you get in these enterprises and actually get them to adopt and use AI?

speaker: SPEAKER_00
